CONSTRUCT THE WITNESS EXPLICITLY OR WEAKEN THE ITEM: if a clean explicit $\varphi$ cannot be exhibited with the machinery of this page, replace this false statement with the weaker and fully provable one that the substitution identity requires $f\circ\varphi$ to be integrable, and refute the version that omits continuity of $f$ by a two-line undefinedness argument. Do not publish a witness that has not been checked; an honest weaker item is preferred.

items.title: For every integrable $f$ on $[a,b]$, the integral function $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ satisfies $F' = f$ on $[a,b]$
items.strategy: refutation by the sign function of [[cex-an-integrable-function-with-no-primitive]]: there $F(x) = \lvert x\rvert - 1$, which is not differentiable at $0$, so $F' = f$ fails at the single point where $f$ is discontinuous. A second, sharper witness: any integrable $f$ that differs from a continuous $g$ at one point has the same $F$ as $g$ ([[lem-changing-a-function-at-finitely-many-points]]), so $F' = g \ne f$ at that point -- this shows the failure is not exotic and cannot be repaired by any hypothesis weaker than continuity at the point. State the true theorem, [[thm-ftc-first-part]], whose hypothesis is continuity AT THE POINT and nowhere else.

title: $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a Normed Space; Vector-Valued Functions

items.title: A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
items.strategy: the page's opening definition, and it is where the SEAM with the published metric theory is fixed rather than left to chance. A norm on a vector space $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-vector-space]]) is $\lVert\cdot\rVert : V \to \mathbb{R}$ with (N1) $\lVert v\rVert = 0$ iff $v = 0$, (N2) $\lVert\lambda v\rVert = \lvert\lambda\rvert\lVert v\rVert$, (N3) the triangle inequality. NONNEGATIVITY IS NOT AN AXIOM, exactly as in [[def-metric-space]]: derive it from (N2) and (N3) ($0 = \lVert v-v\rVert \le 2\lVert v\rVert$), and say that the verification of a candidate norm therefore has three things to check, mirroring [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]. Then prove the DICTIONARY CLAUSE: $d(u,v) := \lVert u-v\rVert$ is a metric on $V$ in the sense of [[def-metric-space]], and it is translation invariant and absolutely homogeneous, which an arbitrary metric need not be. Say plainly that not every metric on a vector space arises this way and give the reason a reader will need later (an arbitrary metric fails homogeneity); the bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]] is the published example, cite it. Values are real, never $+\infty$, as [[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] fixed for metrics. LANDMARK.

items.title: The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: concrete definition with its algebra proved inline; NO abstract inner-product-space theory is developed, and the reason is recorded. $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] on the von Neumann natural $n$, so $x_k := x(k)$ for $k<n$, and $\langle x,y\rangle := \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. VALID FOR EVERY $n$ INCLUDING $n = 0$, where it is the empty sum $0$ -- unlike the metric $d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which needs $n \ge 1$; state that contrast here, because it is the first place on the page where the two index regimes diverge. Prove symmetry, bilinearity and positive definiteness ($\langle x,x\rangle = \sum x_k^{2} \ge 0$ with equality iff $x = 0$, by [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]]) directly from the finite-sum laws. Define $\lVert x\rVert_2 := \sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) and record that this is exactly the $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] at $y = 0$. SCOPE NOTE, to be stated in Remarks and reported: the general theory of inner product spaces is planned for a page EARLIER in plan order that is not yet built, so this item defines the concrete Euclidean form only and claims nothing about abstract inner product spaces.

items.title: Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation
items.strategy: direct, and the first clause is a CITATION, not a new proof: [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]] is published at order 16 and already gives the root form and the equality case in the symmetric proportionality sense; read it on disk and restate it in the vector notation of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would be the two-notions defect in its purest form. What IS new: (a) $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ satisfies (N1)-(N3) of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], the triangle inequality following from Cauchy-Schwarz by expanding $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2}$ -- or by citing [[thm-minkowski-finite]] at $p = 2$, and either route is acceptable provided one is chosen and the other mentioned; (b) the PARALLELOGRAM LAW $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2}+\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} = 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2}+2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2}$, by bilinearity; (c) POLARISATION $\langle x,y\rangle = \tfrac14\bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2}-\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\bigr)$, which says the inner product is recoverable from the norm. Clauses (b) and (c) are what the companion page uses to show that $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ comes from no inner product. LANDMARK.

items.title: The $p$-norms $\lVert x\rVert_p$ for rational $p \ge 1$, and $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$
items.strategy: definition, with TWO hypotheses that are not decoration and must both be stated where the object is introduced. (1) THE EXPONENT IS RATIONAL. $\lVert x\rVert_p := \bigl(\sum_{k<n}\lvert x_k\rvert^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}$ uses [[def-rational-power]], which is defined for rational exponents and nonnegative bases only; real exponents do not exist in this library at this point in the reading order ([[rem-real-exponents-deferred]]), and [[thm-minkowski-finite]] is itself stated for rational $p \ge 1$ for exactly that reason -- read it on disk. Do not write 'for $p \in [1,\infty)$'. (2) $\lVert x\rVert_\infty := \max\{\lvert x_k\rvert : k<n\}$ REQUIRES $n \ge 1$, since at $n = 0$ it is a maximum over the empty set; this is the same restriction [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries and for the same reason, and it propagates to everything on this page mentioning $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$. Existence of the maximum is [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] with [[def-max-min]]. Record $\lVert x\rVert_1$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2$ as the cases $p = 1, 2$ and note $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ agrees with [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]'s.

items.title: Each $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the induced metrics are exactly $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ of the published metric-spaces page
items.strategy: direct, and THIS IS THE DICTIONARY ITEM THAT PREVENTS THE LEVEL-7 TWO-NOTIONS-OF-OPEN DEFECT FROM RECURRING HERE. Clause 1: (N1) and (N2) are computations from [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] and [[lem-rational-power-laws]]; (N3) is [[thm-minkowski-finite]] for rational $p \ge 1$, and the separate elementary argument for $p = \infty$ (a max of sums is at most the sum of maxes), which needs $n \ge 1$. Clause 2, the dictionary: for $p \in \{1,2\}$ and for $\infty$, $\lVert x-y\rVert_p = d_p(x,y)$ where $d_1,d_2,d_\infty$ are the PUBLISHED metrics of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]; the two sides are the same expression, so the proof is a one-line comparison of the definitions -- but the item must exist, because without it the library holds a norm-induced metric and a separately published metric on the same set with no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which is meant. CONSEQUENCE, stated here and used repeatedly below: every published theorem about $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ -- completeness [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]], Heine-Borel [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], the compactness equivalences [[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] -- applies verbatim to the normed space of this page, WITH THEIR HYPOTHESIS $n \ge 1$ INHERITED UNCHANGED.

items.title: Equivalent norms, and the dictionary with equivalent metrics
items.strategy: definition plus a bridge clause. Two norms on $V$ are EQUIVALENT when there are reals $c, C > 0$ with $c\lVert v\rVert \le \lVert v\rVert' \le C\lVert v\rVert$ for every $v$. Prove that this is an equivalence relation (the reflexive and symmetric clauses are immediate; transitivity multiplies constants) and prove the DICTIONARY CLAUSE against [[def-equivalent-metrics]]: equivalent norms induce STRONGLY equivalent metrics in the sense of the published [[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]], hence the same open sets, the same convergent sequences, the same Cauchy sequences and the same uniformly continuous maps. READ [[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]] ON DISK BEFORE STATING WHICH TIER OF EQUIVALENCE IS MEANT: that item distinguishes topological equivalence, uniform equivalence and Lipschitz/strong equivalence, and the norm condition gives the strongest of them; asserting the wrong tier is a citation defect of exactly the dominant class. Note that the converse fails: a metric equivalent to a norm metric need not come from a norm, [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]] being the published witness.

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ every norm $N$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $N(x) \le C\lVert x\rVert_1$ and is Lipschitz, hence continuous, for $d_2$
items.strategy: direct, and it is the half of the norm-equivalence theorem that costs no compactness. Expand $x = \sum_{k<n} x_k e_k$ in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], published, with the coordinate clause giving exactly $x_k = x(k)$ -- read clause 3 before citing) and apply (N2) and (N3) repeatedly: $N(x) \le \sum_{k<n}\lvert x_k\rvert N(e_k) \le C\lVert x\rVert_1$ with $C := \max\{N(e_k) : k<n\}$, a maximum over a nonempty finite set because $n \ge 1$ ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). The repeated triangle inequality is an induction on $n$ -- do it, or cite the finite-sum form if one is available for a general norm, but do not wave. Then $\lvert N(x)-N(y)\rvert \le N(x-y) \le C\lVert x-y\rVert_1 \le C\,\iota(n)^{1/2}\lVert x-y\rVert_2$ (the reverse triangle inequality for a norm, proved from (N3) exactly as [[lem-metric-reverse-triangle]] is for a metric, plus the comparison $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1 \le \iota(n)^{1/2}\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ from [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]] applied with the constant list $1$). So $N$ is Lipschitz for $d_2$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]) and continuous ([[thm-metric-regularity-hierarchy]], [[def-metric-continuity]]). STATE THE COMPARISON CHAIN $\lVert x\rVert_\infty \le \lVert x\rVert_2 \le \lVert x\rVert_1 \le \iota(n)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as a separate clause, with each inequality proved and each requiring $n \ge 1$ where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ appears.

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ all norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equivalent
items.strategy: direct, by compactness of the unit sphere, and the hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from every step. Let $N$ be a norm; by [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] it is continuous for $d_2$ and bounded above by $C\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ after rescaling the constant. The sphere $S := \{x : \lVert x\rVert_2 = 1\}$ is closed (preimage of a point under a continuous map, [[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]), hence COMPACT by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2, and NONEMPTY because $n \ge 1$ gives $e_0 \in S$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) -- state the nonemptiness, it is exactly where $n \ge 1$ enters a second time and where a proof for $n = 0$ would silently break. By [[thm-extreme-value-metric]] the continuous $N$ attains a minimum $c$ on $S$, and $c > 0$ by (N1) since $0 \notin S$. Homogeneity (N2) transfers the two bounds from $S$ to all of $\mathbb{R}^n$: for $x \ne 0$ apply them to $x/\lVert x\rVert_2$; the case $x = 0$ is separate and trivial. Conclude equivalence with $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, hence with each other by transitivity ([[def-equivalent-norms]]). SAY WHAT FAILS IN INFINITE DIMENSIONS and that the companion page carries a witness; phrase it as a statement about this proof (the sphere is no longer compact), not as a claim about spaces the library has not built. LANDMARK.

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ converges iff each coordinate sequence converges, is Cauchy iff each coordinate sequence is Cauchy, and $\mathbb{R}^n$ is complete in every norm
items.strategy: direct, from the comparison chain and then a citation. Clauses 1 and 2 follow from $\lVert x\rVert_\infty \le \lVert x\rVert_2 \le \iota(n)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]): the $\infty$-norm bounds each coordinate and is bounded by the Euclidean norm, so the two convergence notions squeeze each other. Use [[def-metric-convergence]] and [[def-cauchy-in-metric]] as the definitions, and [[thm-metric-limits-unique]]... check the published id ([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]) before citing. CLAUSE 3 IS A CITATION AND MUST NOT BE REPROVED: [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2 is published and states completeness of $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ FOR $n \ge 1$ ONLY; combine it with [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] and the dictionary of [[def-equivalent-norms]] to get completeness in every norm. DO NOT CITE THE PUBLISHED THEOREM FOR ALL $n$: this is the explicit level-8 instruction carried in the prose scaffold, and $n = 0$ is excluded because $d_\infty$, not the theorem, is what fails there. State the $n = 0$ situation once, correctly and separately: $\mathbb{R}^0$ is the zero vector space with a unique element, the zero norm is its only norm, and everything is trivially true -- but it is NOT covered by the published theorem, so it is asserted here from scratch or not at all. LANDMARK.

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a convergent subsequence
items.strategy: direct, assembled from published theorems and NOT reproved by bisection. A bounded sequence lies in a closed bounded set, for instance a closed ball, which is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2; a compact metric space is sequentially compact by [[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] -- read that item on disk and cite the exact clause, since it lists several equivalent forms and their choice costs differ. Note the CHOICE LEDGER, in the style of [[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]]: [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no choice, while the general implication from compact to sequentially compact may; say which is used here and record it, rather than leaving the reader to guess. The prose scaffold's line 'Heine-Borel in $\mathbb{R}^n$ by bisection' describes work ALREADY PUBLISHED at order 120; this page cites it and adds only the sequential corollary. Also record the relation to the published one-dimensional [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]], which is the case $n = 1$ under the identification of $\mathbb{R}^1$ with $\mathbb{R}$ -- state that identification explicitly, since $\mathbb{R}^1$ is a set of functions $1 \to \mathbb{R}$ and is not literally $\mathbb{R}$.

items.title: Vector-valued functions $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^m$, their limits and continuity, with the dictionary to the metric notions
items.strategy: definition whose whole job is to AVOID minting a third notion of continuity. For $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ (or $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$) and $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^m$ with $m \ge 1$, define the limit and continuity by the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ conditions with $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ in the codomain, and then PROVE, not assert, that these are exactly [[def-metric-continuity]] and the metric limit for the metrics of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], via [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]. Cite [[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]] as the precedent: the library already bridged the real and metric notions once and this item is the same move one dimension up. Define the components $f_i := \pi_i \circ f$ for $i<m$, where $\pi_i(y) := y_i$; note $\pi_i$ is $1$-Lipschitz since $\lvert y_i\rvert \le \lVert y\rVert_2$. Everything is stated for $m \ge 1$; at $m = 0$ the codomain has one point and every map is continuous, which is true but is not what the page is about -- say so once and move on.

items.title: A vector-valued function has a limit, or is continuous, if and only if each of its components does
items.strategy: direct, from [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]'s comparison of norms, or directly from $\lvert y_i\rvert \le \lVert y\rVert_2 \le \sum_{j<m}\lvert y_j\rvert$. Give both directions explicitly: one is a single inequality, the other needs the sum over $m$ components and hence a $\delta$ chosen for $\varepsilon/\iota(m)$ -- and that division requires $m \ge 1$, which is the standing hypothesis. State the immediate consequences that later items use: the algebra of continuous vector-valued functions (sums, scalar multiples, and $\langle f,g\rangle$, using bilinearity of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] componentwise), and that $x \mapsto \lVert x\rVert$ is continuous for every norm ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]). Do not restate the metric algebra results; cite them.

items.title: The derivative and the Riemann integral of a function $[a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$, defined componentwise and characterised intrinsically
items.strategy: one definition with two halves, each carrying its own well-definedness. DERIVATIVE: for $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and $c$ a limit point of $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, $f'(c)$ is the limit of the difference quotient $(f(x)-f(c))/(x-c)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); the limit is unique ([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), and by [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] it exists iff each $f_i'(c)$ exists, with $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$. Give the intrinsic form FIRST and the componentwise form as a theorem-clause, not the other way round -- the intrinsic form is the one that survives to the total derivative later. INTEGRAL: for $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$ define $f$ to be integrable when each $f_i$ is, and $\int_a^b f := \bigl(\int_a^b f_0,\dots,\int_a^b f_{m-1}\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the component integrals being those of [[def-darboux-integral]] with the orientation convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. Well-definedness is the observation that a tuple of reals is an element of $\mathbb{R}^m$, i.e. a function $m \to \mathbb{R}$ -- write it as such, since $\mathbb{R}^m$ is a function space and not a set of tuples in this library. Record linearity of both operations from [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] componentwise.

items.title: For $a \le b$ and integrable $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$, $\lVert f\rVert_2$ is integrable and $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2$
items.strategy: direct, by the inner-product trick, which is shorter and sharper than any componentwise estimate. Put $v := \int_a^b f \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then $\lVert v\rVert_2^{2} = \langle v,v\rangle = \sum_{i<m} v_i\int_a^b f_i = \int_a^b \langle v,f\rangle$ by [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]] applied $m$ times and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; by Cauchy-Schwarz ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]) the integrand is at most $\lVert v\rVert_2\lVert f\rVert_2$ pointwise, so [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] gives $\lVert v\rVert_2^{2} \le \lVert v\rVert_2\int_a^b\lVert f\rVert_2$; divide by $\lVert v\rVert_2$ WHEN IT IS NONZERO and handle $v = 0$ separately -- that case split is mandatory and is where the usual textbook proof is silently incomplete. INTEGRABILITY OF $\lVert f\rVert_2$ IS A SEPARATE OBLIGATION and must be discharged before the estimate: each $f_i$ is integrable, so $f_i^{2}$ and the sum are ([[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]), and the square root is continuous on $[0,\infty)$, so [[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]] applies. The hypothesis $a \le b$ is needed because the orientation convention flips the inequality; say so, exactly as the scalar case does. LANDMARK.

items.title: The mean value inequality: if $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is continuous and differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\lVert f'\rVert_2 \le M$, then $\lVert f(b)-f(a)\rVert_2 \le M(b-a)$
items.strategy: direct, by reducing to the scalar mean value theorem with a fixed auxiliary vector -- the proof that needs NO integrability hypothesis and therefore no dependence on the integral half of this page. Put $u := f(b)-f(a)$ and $\varphi(t) := \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, a real-valued function on $[a,b]$, continuous by [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] and differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'(t) = \langle u, f'(t)\rangle$ by [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] applied to the finite sum defining the inner product. By [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] there is $\xi$ with $\varphi(b)-\varphi(a) = \varphi'(\xi)(b-a)$, that is $\lVert u\rVert_2^{2} = \langle u, f'(\xi)\rangle (b-a) \le \lVert u\rVert_2 M (b-a)$ by [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Divide by $\lVert u\rVert_2$ when nonzero and treat $u = 0$ separately. THE EQUALITY FORM IS FALSE FOR $m \ge 2$: there need be NO $\xi$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$, and the companion page carries the witness. Say that here in exactly one sentence, WITHOUT asserting the false statement as though it were a theorem, and note that the $\xi$ produced above depends on $u$ and is therefore not a mean value point for $f$. LANDMARK.

items.title: If $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is differentiable with integrable $f'$ then $\int_a^b f' = f(b)-f(a)$; and a bounded derivative makes $f$ Lipschitz
items.strategy: direct, componentwise from [[thm-ftc-second-part]] together with [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]'s componentwise clause, then the Lipschitz bound from [[thm-mean-value-inequality]] applied on each subinterval $[s,t] \subseteq [a,b]$. State the Lipschitz conclusion in the sense of [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]] for the metrics of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], not informally. Note the alternative derivation of the mean value inequality from [[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]] when $f'$ is integrable, and say why the theorem above is proved the other way instead: it needs no integrability, so it applies to every differentiable $f$, and the companion page's witness for the failure of the equality form is differentiable but is not assumed integrable. That comparison is the item's real content and should be written out rather than left implicit.

items.title: Series of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, absolute convergence, rearrangement, and the set of rearrangement sums
items.strategy: definition, with an explicit agreement clause against the published one-dimensional theory. For a sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ the partial sums are $s_N := \sum_{k<N} x_k$ (the finite sum in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$, which is the pointwise finite sum of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 1 -- cite it rather than minting a third finite sum), and $\sum x_k$ CONVERGES to $s$ when $s_N \to s$ in $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]); it converges ABSOLUTELY when the real series $\sum\lVert x_k\rVert_2$ converges ([[def-series]]). A REARRANGEMENT is $\sum x_{\sigma(k)}$ for a bijection $\sigma : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, verbatim as in the published [[def-rearrangement-and-unconditional-convergence]]; the SET OF REARRANGEMENT SUMS is $\mathcal{S}(x) := \{\,s : \text{some rearrangement converges to } s\,\}$. AGREEMENT CLAUSE, mandatory: at $n = 1$, under the identification of $\mathbb{R}^1$ with $\mathbb{R}$, these are exactly [[def-series]] and [[def-rearrangement-and-unconditional-convergence]] and $\mathcal{S}$ is exactly the set the published [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] calls $\mathcal{S}(a)$; state the identification, since $\mathbb{R}^1$ is a function space and not literally $\mathbb{R}$. Everything here needs $n \ge 1$ because $d_2$ does.

items.title: An absolutely convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^n$ converges, and every rearrangement converges to the same sum
items.strategy: direct, in two clauses, both by reduction to the published one-dimensional theory rather than by re-running its proofs. Clause 1: absolute convergence gives a Cauchy sequence of partial sums, by the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]) and the Cauchy criterion for the real series [[thm-series-cauchy-criterion]]; then completeness ([[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]) gives convergence. Clause 2: each coordinate series converges absolutely because $\lvert (x_k)_i\rvert \le \lVert x_k\rVert_2$ and [[thm-direct-comparison-test]], so [[thm-dirichlet-rearrangement]] applies coordinatewise, and [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]] reassembles the sum. State the consequence in the form the next items use: if $\sum x_k$ converges absolutely then $\mathcal{S}(x)$ is the single point $\{\sum x_k\}$. Note that [[lem-absolute-convergence-implies-convergence]] is the published one-dimensional statement and that this theorem is its $\mathbb{R}^n$ analogue, NOT a generalisation of its proof.

items.title: The subspace $\Gamma$ of directions along which a series converges absolutely, and its orthogonal complement $\Gamma^{\perp}$
items.strategy: definition, PHRASED WITH THE INNER PRODUCT AND NOT WITH LINEAR FUNCTIONALS, and that is a deliberate design decision forced by plan order: the page that introduces linear maps and dual spaces sits earlier in plan order but is not built, so no linear-map vocabulary is available here. For a convergent series $\sum x_k$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ set $\Gamma := \{\,a \in \mathbb{R}^n : \sum_k \lvert\langle a, x_k\rangle\rvert \text{ converges}\,\}$ and $\Gamma^{\perp} := \{\,y \in \mathbb{R}^n : \langle a,y\rangle = 0 \text{ for every } a \in \Gamma\,\}$. PROVE BOTH ARE LINEAR SUBSPACES ([[def-linear-subspace]], [[lem-linear-subspace-criterion]]): for $\Gamma$ use bilinearity and [[lem-series-linearity]] with [[thm-direct-comparison-test]]; for $\Gamma^{\perp}$ use bilinearity alone. Record $0 \in \Gamma$ always, and $\Gamma = \mathbb{R}^n$ exactly when the series converges absolutely (one direction by comparison with $\lVert x_k\rVert_2$ using [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], the other by testing against the standard basis and [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]'s comparison chain) -- that equivalence is what makes the next theorem contain [[thm-absolute-convergence-in-rn]] as a special case. Define AFFINE SUBSPACE as a coset $s + W$ of a linear subspace, since the library has no such notion yet, and prove the coset is determined by $W$ and any of its points.

items.title: Steinitz's polygonal confinement theorem: finitely many vectors of norm at most $1$ summing to $0$ can be ordered so that every partial sum has norm at most $n$
items.strategy: constructive, and the proof is fully available from published material; scaffold it in five named stages and check each. STATEMENT: let $n \ge 1$, let $v : m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $\lVert v_i\rVert_2 \le 1$ for every $i<m$ and $\sum_{i<m} v_i = 0$; then there is a bijection $\pi : m \to m$ with $\lVert\sum_{i<k} v_{\pi(i)}\rVert_2 \le \iota(n)$ for every $k \le m$. (1) If $m \le n$ every partial sum has norm at most $\iota(k) \le \iota(n)$ by the triangle inequality; assume $m > n$. (2) For $n \le k \le m$ let $\Lambda_k := \{\lambda : m \to [0,1] \mid \sum_i \lambda_i v_i = 0,\ \sum_i \lambda_i = \iota(k-n)\}$ RELATIVE TO A SUBSET $A_k$ (see 3). $\Lambda_m$ contains the constant $\iota(m-n)/\iota(m)$, since $\sum v_i = 0$. (3) DESCENDING CONSTRUCTION: build $A_m \supseteq A_{m-1} \supseteq \dots \supseteq A_n$ with $\lvert A_k\rvert = k$ and $\lambda^{k}$ supported in $A_k$, in $[0,1]^{A_k}$, with $\sum_{i \in A_k}\lambda^k_i v_i = 0$ and $\sum_{i\in A_k}\lambda^k_i = \iota(k-n)$. Given $A_k,\lambda^k$, the feasible set for $k-1$ is nonempty (scale $\lambda^k$ by $\iota(k-1-n)/\iota(k-n)$; the case $k-n = 0$ does not arise since the construction stops at $k = n$). (4) THE KEY LEMMA, and it is pure linear algebra: among the feasible $\lambda$ choose one with the FEWEST coordinates in the open interval $(0,1)$ -- legitimate because a nonempty set of naturals has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]). If that number were at least $n+2$, the vectors $(v_i,1) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ indexed by the fractional coordinates would be more than $\dim \mathbb{R}^{n+1} = n+1$ in number, hence linearly dependent ([[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[def-dimension]]); a nontrivial dependence $\mu$ gives $\sum\mu_i v_i = 0$ and $\sum\mu_i = 0$, and moving $\lambda + t\mu$ to the nearest $t$ at which some fractional coordinate reaches $0$ or $1$ (a minimum over a nonempty finite set of reals, [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]) keeps feasibility and strictly reduces the count -- contradiction. So at most $n+1$ coordinates are fractional. (5) THE SUPPORT BOUND, the step that makes the nesting work and the one an inattentive proof omits: $\#\{i : \lambda_i = 1\} \le \sum_i\lambda_i = k-1-n$, so $\#\mathrm{supp}(\lambda) \le (k-1-n)+(n+1) = k$; and equality would force the fractional coordinates to sum to $0$ while each is strictly positive, which is impossible, so $\#\mathrm{supp}(\lambda) \le k-1$ and an $A_{k-1} \subseteq A_k$ of size $k-1$ containing the support exists. (6) THE ORDERING: enumerate $A_n$ first in any order, then the single element of $A_{k}\setminus A_{k-1}$ for $k = n+1,\dots,m$ in increasing $k$. For $k \le n$ the partial sum has norm at most $\iota(k)\le\iota(n)$; for $k \ge n$ the partial sum is $\sum_{i\in A_k} v_i = \sum_{i\in A_k}(1-\lambda^k_i)v_i$, whose norm is at most $\sum_{i\in A_k}(1-\lambda^k_i) = \iota(k) - \iota(k-n) = \iota(n)$. Every sum here is a sum over a finite index set; if the counting page's index-set sum is not among this page's declared prerequisites, index by a chosen enumeration and use [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] instead. LANDMARK.

items.title: The set of rearrangement sums of a convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a nonempty subset of the affine subspace $s + \Gamma^{\perp}$
items.strategy: direct, and it is the containment half of the Levy-Steinitz theorem; SCOPE THE CLAIM EXACTLY AND DO NOT OVERSTATE THE TITLE, since a title claiming more than the proof gives is a fatal defect. Let $\sum x_k$ converge to $s$. Nonemptiness: $s \in \mathcal{S}(x)$, via the identity bijection. Containment: let $t \in \mathcal{S}(x)$, so $\sum x_{\sigma(k)} = t$ for some bijection $\sigma$, and let $a \in \Gamma$. The real series $\sum\langle a,x_k\rangle$ converges absolutely by definition of $\Gamma$, so by the published [[thm-dirichlet-rearrangement]] every rearrangement of it has the same sum; and $\langle a,\cdot\rangle$ is continuous ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], or directly by Cauchy-Schwarz) and additive on finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 1), so $\langle a,t\rangle = \sum_k\langle a,x_{\sigma(k)}\rangle = \sum_k\langle a,x_k\rangle = \langle a,s\rangle$. Hence $\langle a, t-s\rangle = 0$ for every $a \in \Gamma$, that is $t - s \in \Gamma^{\perp}$. State the two extreme cases as clauses, because they are exactly the published one-dimensional dichotomy seen from here: if the series converges absolutely then $\Gamma = \mathbb{R}^n$, $\Gamma^{\perp} = \{0\}$ and $\mathcal{S}(x) = \{s\}$ ([[thm-absolute-convergence-in-rn]]); at $n = 1$ a conditionally convergent series has $\Gamma = \{0\}$ and $\Gamma^{\perp} = \mathbb{R}$, and the published [[thm-riemann-series-theorem]] says the containment is then an EQUALITY. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED, and must be said in Remarks in exactly these terms: this theorem gives containment only; whether $\mathcal{S}(x)$ is all of $s+\Gamma^{\perp}$ for $n \ge 2$ is not settled here, and no assertion about it, in either direction, is made anywhere on this page. Declare [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] nowhere in `deps` -- it is a published remark on an earlier page and the edge runs the other way, as a forward reference to be added there. LANDMARK.

items.title: Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order
items.strategy: the page ledger, and on this page it carries more weight than usual because three separate scope decisions were taken. Record: (1) THE $n \ge 1$ HYPOTHESIS, where it comes from ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $d_\infty$ only there) and exactly which items inherit it -- list them; note that [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the vector space structure are fine at $n = 0$, so the boundary is between the algebra and the metric, not between statements a reader would guess. (2) THE EXPONENT IN $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ IS RATIONAL, because real exponents do not exist at this point in the reading order ([[rem-real-exponents-deferred]]); every $p$-norm statement on this page carries it. (3) $\mathbb{R}^n$ IS A FUNCTION SPACE, the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-function-space]]), so $\mathbb{R}^1$ is not literally $\mathbb{R}$ and every comparison with the one-dimensional theory goes through the stated identification. (4) WHAT IS TAKEN UP ELSEWHERE, phrased as reading order and never as a claim about the library as a whole: the operator norm and the fact that linear maps are Lipschitz belong with linear maps, which are introduced on a page earlier in plan order that is not yet built; the general theory of inner product spaces and orthogonality likewise; uniform convergence, the total derivative and the integral in $\mathbb{R}^m$ all come later in this track. (5) THE OPEN HALF OF THE REARRANGEMENT QUESTION: [[thm-rearrangement-sums-lie-in-an-affine-subspace]] proves containment and the page asserts nothing about the reverse inclusion for $n \ge 2$; the published [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] on the series page raised the question and this page answers the part it can. State that plainly; do NOT state the classical answer, in any form, and do not create a recorded-not-proved item for it.

title: $\mathbb{R}^n$ as a Normed Space: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $f(t) = (t^{2}, t^{3})$ on $[0,1]$: no $\xi$ satisfies $f(1)-f(0) = f'(\xi)$
items.strategy: counterexample, refuting the equality form of the mean value theorem for $m \ge 2$ and confirming that [[thm-mean-value-inequality]] is the correct statement. $f(1)-f(0) = (1,1)$ and $f'(t) = (2t,3t^{2})$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]] componentwise, via [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); $2\xi = 1$ forces $\xi = 1/\iota(2)$, and then $3\xi^{2} = 3/\iota(4) \ne 1$. Do the arithmetic in $\mathbb{R}$ with the canonical naturals visible. CHOSEN DELIBERATELY OVER THE CLASSICAL WITNESS: the crispest classical example is $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi]$, and the trigonometric functions are introduced later in the reading order, so a polynomial curve is used instead; record that substitution here rather than in a scaffold note, since a reader who knows the classical example will look for it. Then CHECK the inequality form on the same curve: $\lVert f(1)-f(0)\rVert_2 = \sqrt{2}$ and $\sup\lVert f'\rVert_2 = \sqrt{13}$ on $[0,1]$, so the inequality holds with room to spare.

items.title: The comparison constants between $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$, and vectors attaining each
items.strategy: computation, and the value is that every constant is shown SHARP by an attaining vector, which the general theorem [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] does not supply. On $\mathbb{R}^{2}$: $\lVert x\rVert_\infty \le \lVert x\rVert_2 \le \lVert x\rVert_1 \le \iota(2)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ and $\lVert x\rVert_1 \le \sqrt{2}\lVert x\rVert_2$; exhibit $e_0$ (attaining the first, third-from-left and the outer chain at one end) and $(1,1)$ (attaining $\lVert x\rVert_1 = 2$, $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \sqrt{2}$, $\lVert x\rVert_\infty = 1$, which is the extreme case of both the $\sqrt{2}$ and the $\iota(2)$ constants). Verify each inequality from [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]'s chain and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]. Also compute the unit balls' inclusions to make the geometry explicit.

items.title: $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ violates the parallelogram law, so it is induced by no inner product
items.strategy: counterexample with a two-line computation and a precise conclusion. Take $x = e_0$, $y = e_1$: $\lVert x+y\rVert_1^{2}+\lVert x-y\rVert_1^{2} = 4+4 = 8$ while $2\lVert x\rVert_1^{2}+2\lVert y\rVert_1^{2} = 4$. Since every norm arising from an inner product satisfies the parallelogram law ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] clause (b)), no inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ induces $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$. STATE THE LOGIC PRECISELY: the page proves the parallelogram law only for the Euclidean inner product, so the conclusion available here is about norms of that form; a general converse (the Jordan-von Neumann theorem, that the parallelogram law characterises inner-product norms) is not proved on this page and must not be asserted. Note also that $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ IS equivalent to $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ by [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] -- equivalence of norms is a metric statement and says nothing about inner products, which is the point worth making.

items.title: $g(x,y) = xy/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, extended by $g(0,0)=0$, is continuous in each variable separately and not continuous at the origin
items.strategy: counterexample. Continuity in each variable separately at the origin: $g(x,0) = 0$ and $g(0,y) = 0$ for all $x,y$, so both partial functions are constant. Discontinuity at the origin: along the line $y = x$ the value is $1/\iota(2)$ for $x \ne 0$, and points of that line come arbitrarily close to the origin, so no $\delta$ works ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]], [[def-metric-continuity]]); or use the sequential criterion with $(1/\iota(k+1), 1/\iota(k+1))$ and [[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]]. Continuity away from the origin follows from [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] and [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]. THE POINT IS THAT SEPARATE CONTINUITY IS STRICTLY WEAKER, and this is the first place in the library where a function of several real variables appears, so state the domain as $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with the metric of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] rather than informally.

items.title: A convergent sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and the integral $\int_0^1 (1, t, t^{2})$, computed componentwise
items.strategy: computation exercising both halves of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] and [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]. Take $x^{(k)} = (1/\iota(k+1),\ 1 - 1/\iota(k+1),\ 2)$ and show $x^{(k)} \to (0,1,2)$ by the componentwise criterion, checking that the $\varepsilon$ for the vector is obtained from the three coordinate $\varepsilon$'s exactly as the theorem's proof does. Then compute $\int_0^1 (1,t,t^{2}) = (1, 1/\iota(2), 1/\iota(3))$ by [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] componentwise, and CHECK the norm inequality [[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]] on this example numerically: $\lVert\int f\rVert_2$ against $\int\lVert f\rVert_2$, bounding the latter from below by a crude estimate rather than evaluating it, since its exact value needs machinery not available here. Say that the inequality is strict here and why.

items.title: Steinitz's confinement bound realised on an explicit list of six unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ summing to zero
items.strategy: verification, and it makes an abstract existence proof concrete. Take six vectors of norm at most $1$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ summing to $0$ -- for instance $\pm e_0, \pm e_1$ together with $\pm(1,1)/\sqrt{2}$ -- exhibit an ordering whose partial sums all have norm at most $\iota(2)$, and exhibit a BAD ordering whose partial sums exceed $1$, so that the theorem is seen to say something. Then trace one step of the descending construction of [[thm-steinitz-polygonal-confinement]] on this list: write down $A_6$, one $\lambda^{6}$, and the resulting $A_5$, checking the support bound $\#\mathrm{supp} \le k-1$ that the proof turns on. An example that only asserts the bound would be worth much less than one that exhibits the construction.

items.title: A convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $\Gamma$ a line and $\Gamma^{\perp}$ a line, computed from the definition
items.strategy: computation, and it is the example that makes [[def-the-space-of-summing-directions]] concrete. Take $x_k := \bigl((-1)^{k}/\iota(k+1),\ 0\bigr)$: the series converges by the alternating series test ([[thm-alternating-series-test]]) in the first coordinate and trivially in the second. For $a = (a_0,a_1)$, $\langle a,x_k\rangle = a_0(-1)^{k}/\iota(k+1)$, so $\sum\lvert\langle a,x_k\rangle\rvert$ converges iff $a_0 = 0$ (harmonic divergence, [[thm-p-series-rational]] at $p=1$ or [[thm-cauchy-condensation]]). Hence $\Gamma = \{(0,a_1)\}$, a line, and $\Gamma^{\perp} = \{(y_0,0)\}$, a line. So [[thm-rearrangement-sums-lie-in-an-affine-subspace]] confines every rearrangement sum to the horizontal line through $s$ -- and, since the second coordinate is identically $0$, that confinement is visibly sharp in the trivial direction. Note what this example does NOT decide: whether every point of that line is attained. Say so; do not assert it.

items.title: If a convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ does not converge absolutely, then every point of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the sum of some rearrangement of it
items.strategy: refutation, and it is the item that stops a reader generalising [[thm-riemann-series-theorem]] by analogy -- the exact expectation the published [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] warns against. Use the series of [[ex-gamma-and-its-complement-computed-for-a-plane-series]]: it converges, it does not converge absolutely (its norms are $1/\iota(k+1)$, whose series diverges), and every rearrangement has second coordinate $0$, so no point off the horizontal line through $s$ is a rearrangement sum. That refutes the statement without needing any part of the classical higher-dimensional theorem, which is the point: the refutation is elementary and complete. Note that [[thm-rearrangement-sums-lie-in-an-affine-subspace]] explains it structurally, $\Gamma^{\perp}$ being a proper subspace, and that the one-dimensional case is genuinely different because there $\Gamma = \{0\}$ forces $\Gamma^{\perp} = \mathbb{R}$.

items.title: All norms on a real vector space are equivalent
items.strategy: refutation on an infinite-dimensional space built from published material only. Let $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of sequences with only finitely many nonzero terms; it is a linear subspace of the function space $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ ([[def-function-space]], [[lem-linear-subspace-criterion]]) -- prove that, it is two lines. On $V$ define $N_1(v) := \sum_{k<K}\lvert v_k\rvert$ for any $K$ beyond the last nonzero index (well defined: prove the value does not depend on $K$, which is where finiteness of the support is spent) and $N_\infty(v) := \max\{\lvert v_k\rvert : k<K\}$; both are norms by the same computations as [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]. The vectors $u^{(m)} := e_0+\dots+e_{m-1}$ have $N_1(u^{(m)}) = \iota(m)$ and $N_\infty(u^{(m)}) = 1$, so no constant $C$ satisfies $N_1 \le C N_\infty$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]). STATE THE HYPOTHESIS THAT FAILS: [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] is about $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n$ a natural number, and its proof spends compactness of the unit sphere, which is a finite-dimensional fact; $V$ is not finite-dimensional ([[def-dimension]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] give the comparison). Do not claim anything about general infinite-dimensional normed spaces, a theory this library has not built.

items.title: In every normed space a closed bounded set is compact
items.strategy: refutation on the same space $V$ of finitely supported sequences used in the previous item, with the norm $N_\infty$. The closed unit ball of $(V,N_\infty)$ is closed and bounded ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) but not compact: the standard unit vectors $e_k$ all lie in it and satisfy $N_\infty(e_j - e_k) = 1$ for $j \ne k$, so no subsequence is Cauchy ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) and none converges, contradicting sequential compactness ([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]], [[def-metric-compactness-variants]]). STATE WHERE THE PUBLISHED THEOREM'S HYPOTHESIS IS: [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is about $\mathbb{R}^n$ for a natural $n$, and its bisection proof consumes exactly that finiteness. Note as a bonus that the same family shows $(V,N_\infty)$ is not totally bounded ([[def-totally-bounded]]), which is the property the general metric characterisation [[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] identifies as missing.

items.title: A sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose coordinate sequences are each bounded converges
items.strategy: refutation by the smallest possible witness, and it is here to separate two statements that are easy to conflate. Take $n = 1$ and the sequence $x^{(k)} = ((-1)^{k})$: each coordinate is bounded, and the sequence does not converge ([[lem-limit-unique]] with two subsequential limits, or [[thm-convergence-iff-limsup-equals-liminf]]). The TRUE statement in the neighbourhood is [[cor-bolzano-weierstrass-in-rn]]: a bounded sequence has a convergent SUBSEQUENCE, not a limit. Also state the true componentwise statement, [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]] clause 1, which is about convergence and not about boundedness, and point out that the false statement conflates the hypothesis of one with the conclusion of the other.

items.title: A curve for which the mean value inequality is an equality, showing the constant cannot be improved
items.strategy: the positive companion of the first item on this page, and it is what makes [[thm-mean-value-inequality]] sharp rather than merely true. Take $f(t) = (t, 0)$ on $[0,1]$: $\lVert f'\rVert_2 \equiv 1$ and $\lVert f(1)-f(0)\rVert_2 = 1 = 1\cdot(1-0)$. So no constant smaller than $\sup\lVert f'\rVert_2$ works in general, and the inequality is the best possible statement of its shape. Contrast with the first item on this page, where the same inequality is strict; the two together show that the failure of the equality FORM is not a failure of the bound. Compute both norms explicitly.
